context: Two environmental science students discussing a river fieldwork report

cues.t: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Hannah and Raj, discussing a report on their fieldwork on a river. First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
Raj, have you looked at the river data yet? We really need to get this fieldwork report finished.
I have. But before we get to the results, we should explain why we picked that stretch of the River Esk. It's a long way from the campus, after all.

It is. And Dr Mills did offer us a site on the river she's researching, which would have been far easier. No, we chose the Esk because of the old copper mine upstream. It poisoned the river for over a century, and we wanted to find out whether the water had recovered since it closed.
Right. Then there's the method. I thought we'd have trouble getting permission from the landowner, but he couldn't have been more helpful.

And the river didn't flood, even after all that rain. Our only real difficulty was the oxygen meter. It kept giving impossible readings on the first morning, and we lost about three hours before we realised that it needed to be recalibrated.
Don't remind me. Anyway, the results. What surprised you most?

The nitrate levels were higher below the farms, but anyone could have predicted that. What I didn't expect was the mayfly larvae. They're very sensitive to pollution, so I assumed we wouldn't find any near the town. But there were more of them there than anywhere else on the river.
That's fascinating. We should make more of that in the discussion.
Yes. One explanation could be that the town's treatment works has improved so much in recent years.
Possibly, but we'd need far more evidence before we could say that. We should probably mention it as a question for future research.
Definitely. What did Dr Mills say about the draft, by the way?

She liked the tables, and she doesn't think we need to go back and take more samples in the winter, because that's beyond the scope of the project. But she does want us to run a statistical test on the differences between the sites. Without that, we can't claim that they're significant.
Fair enough. So what comes first? Shall I write to the water company about our findings?
That can wait until the report's finished, and the maps are already done. Let's start by entering the last set of readings into the spreadsheet, because we can't do any analysis until that's done.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
Let's look at the methods section. We used five techniques, and we should comment on each of them. Kick sampling first.

You'd think you'd need special training for that, but we learned to do it in about ten minutes. What makes it valuable is that the insects you collect have been living in that spot for months, so they show what the river has been like over a long period, not just on one particular day.
It was certainly the most enjoyable part of the whole trip.
Apart from falling in the river, you mean.
Then the dissolved oxygen probe.

It's reliable once it's been calibrated, but you have to be careful. Oxygen rises during daylight, as the water plants produce it, and it falls again at night, so two readings can differ simply because of the hour they were taken.
What about the nitrate test strips?
They're very convenient, and they cost only a few pence each. The drawback is that you're judging a colour by eye, so the figures you get are only rough.
And the temperature loggers?
We just tied them to a rock and left them there for a month. They took a measurement automatically every ten minutes, day and night, so we ended up with an unbroken record.
Did we lose any of them?
Only one, which was washed downstream during the storm. The other five all worked perfectly.
Finally, the phosphate sampling.
That was the most awkward one. You can't test for it on the riverbank. The bottles have to be kept cold and taken to the university's chemists for testing within twenty-four hours.
Good. I'll start writing that up tonight.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

items.stem: Why did the students choose the site on the River Esk?

options.A: It was close to the university.
options.B: It had a history of pollution.
options.C: Their tutor was doing research there.

items.stem: What problem did the students have during the fieldwork?

options.A: A piece of equipment gave false readings.

items.stem: What surprised Hannah about the results?

options.A: the nitrate levels below the farms
options.B: the number of mayfly larvae near the town
options.C: the oxygen levels in the upper river

items.stem: What does Dr Mills want the students to do?
What will the students do first?

groups.instruction: What do the students say about each method?
groups.limit: Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 26–30.

options.A: It is cheap but not very accurate.
options.B: It cannot be carried out in the field.
options.D: Its results depend on the time of day.
options.E: It requires a long period of training.
options.F: It reflects conditions over several months.
